questions.q: A pyriform, distended gallbladder on examination is a cause of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Shape of gallbladder: pyriform means distended GB — causes are periampullary cancers (obstructive jaundice) and mucocele; a GB mass is the NOT-pyriform variant. (Book p265)

questions.q: A distended (pyriform) gallbladder shows on examination:
questions.exp: Pyriform (distended) GB: O/E — side to side mobility. (Book p265)

questions.q: A gallbladder mass is NOT pyriform and on examination shows:
questions.exp: Shape of gallbladder: not pyriform — GB mass, due to GB cancer; O/E — no side to side mobility. (Book p265)

questions.q: The boundaries of the hepatocystic triangle are:
opts: Inferior edge of liver, common hepatic duct and cystic duct
Cystic artery, cystic duct and common hepatic duct
Inferior edge of liver, cystic artery and cystic duct
Gallbladder neck, cystic artery and common bile duct
questions.exp: Hepatocystic triangle boundaries: inferior edge of liver, common hepatic duct and cystic duct. (Book p265)

questions.q: Calot's triangle is bounded by:
opts: Cystic artery, cystic duct and common hepatic duct
Inferior edge of liver, common hepatic duct and cystic duct
Cystic artery, common bile duct and gallbladder neck
Hepatic artery, cystic duct and cystic plate
questions.exp: Calot's triangle boundaries: cystic artery, cystic duct and common hepatic duct. (Book p265)

questions.q: The content of Calot's triangle is:
questions.exp: Calot's triangle: content — cystic lymph node of Lund. (Book p265)

questions.q: The cystic lymph node of Lund is also known as:
opts: The sentinel node of the gallbladder
questions.exp: Calot's triangle: the cystic lymph node of Lund is the sentinel node of the gallbladder. (Book p265)

questions.q: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the critical view of safety is achieved by dissecting:
questions.exp: Critical view of safety: Calot's triangle is dissected during lap cholecystectomy. (Book p265)

questions.q: In the critical view of safety, which two structures are clipped before the gallbladder is removed?
opts: Cystic artery and common hepatic duct
Cystic duct and common bile duct
Right hepatic artery and cystic duct
questions.exp: Critical view of safety: the cystic artery and cystic duct are clipped, then the gallbladder is removed. (Book p265)

questions.q: Moynihan's hump is:
opts: A tortuous right hepatic artery lying in Calot's triangle
A stone in the cystic duct
A variant of the cystic plate
questions.exp: Moynihan's hump: tortuous (R) hepatic artery lying in Calot's triangle. (Book p265)

questions.q: The cystic artery is a branch of:
questions.exp: Moynihan's hump: cystic artery — branch of the right hepatic artery. (Book p265)

questions.q: The clinical significance of Moynihan's hump is that it may be:
opts: Injured during laparoscopic cholecystectomy causing bleeding
questions.exp: Moynihan's hump: clinical significance — injury during lap cholecystectomy leads to bleeding. (Book p265)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: The cystic plate:
opts: Is the peritoneal lining of the cystic duct
Lies below the liver capsule of segment 2
questions.exp: Cystic plate: covers the gallbladder fossa. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: The cystic plate is a sheet continuous with the liver capsule of which Couinaud segments?
questions.exp: Cystic plate: sheet continuous with the liver capsule of segments 4 and 5. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: Exposure of the cystic plate corresponds to:
questions.exp: Cystic plate: cystic plate exposed — critical view of safety. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: Rouviere's sulcus is located on:
opts: The undersurface of the right lobe of liver
The undersurface of the left lobe
questions.exp: Rouviere's sulcus: undersurface of the right lobe of liver. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: Rouviere's sulcus runs to the right of the hepatic hilum, marking the position of:
questions.exp: Rouviere's sulcus: running to the right of the hepatic hilum — position of the right posterior sectoral pedicle. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: The R4U line runs from:
opts: The roof of Rouviere's sulcus to the base of segment 4
The gallbladder fundus to the umbilicus
The porta hepatis to the IVC
questions.exp: R4U line: roof of the Rouviere sulcus to the base of segment 4. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: In the sequence Rouviere's sulcus leads to segment 4 and then to:
questions.exp: R4U line: Rouviere's sulcus leads to segment 4 and then to the umbilical fissure (U). (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: The common bile duct lies in relation to the R4U line:
opts: Below the line, where it is at risk of injury
Always at the roof of Rouviere's sulcus
questions.exp: Clinical significance: CBD present below the R4U line — injury. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: Doing laparoscopic cholecystectomy above the R4U line:
opts: Increases the risk of CBD injury
Prevents exposure of the cystic plate
questions.exp: Clinical significance: lap cholecystectomy above the line minimises injury. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: Which layer is characteristically ABSENT from the gallbladder wall?
questions.exp: General anatomy: the gallbladder lacks submucosa. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: The subserosal lymphatics of the gallbladder drain into the gallbladder fossa, which explains:
opts: Metastasis of gallbladder cancer into the liver
questions.exp: General anatomy: contains subserosal lymphatics that drain into the GB fossa — metastasis of GB cancer into liver. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: Spread of gallbladder cancer into the liver occurs by all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Lymphatic emboli to the lung only
questions.exp: Note: spread of GB cancer into liver — subserosal lymphatics, direct infiltration and haematogenous spread. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: A Phrygian cap is:
opts: A physiological variant of the gallbladder
questions.exp: Phrygian cap: physiological variant of gallbladder. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: A Phrygian cap:
opts: Is NOT an indication for surgical removal
questions.exp: Phrygian cap: not an indication for surgical removal. (Book p266)

questions.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
questions.q: A Phrygian cap on USG shows:
questions.exp: Phrygian cap USG figure: fundus folded inwards; it does not raise the risk of cancer. (Book p266)

questions.q: The functions of the gallbladder include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Functions: reservoir of bile, secretion of mucin, concentration of bile. (Book p267)

questions.q: Pure cholesterol gallstones have a cholesterol content of:
questions.exp: Gall stones: pure cholesterol stones — >90% cholesterol content. (Book p267)

questions.q: Pure cholesterol gallstones are characteristically:
questions.exp: Gall stones: pure cholesterol stones — solitary. (Book p267)

questions.q: Pigment gallstones contain:
questions.exp: Gall stones: pigment stones — 30-40% cholesterol. (Book p267)

questions.q: The most common stones overall are:
questions.exp: Gall stones: mixed stones — m/c stones overall. (Book p267)

questions.q: Brown pigment stones are seen in:
opts: Infected bile with ascariasis, clonorchiasis and cholangitis
questions.exp: Brown pigment stones: seen in infected bile — ascariasis infection, clonorchiasis infection, cholangitis. (Book p267)

questions.q: The composition of brown pigment stones includes:
opts: Calcium palmitate, calcium stearate and calcium bilirubinate
questions.exp: Brown pigment stones: composition — calcium palmitate, calcium stearate, calcium bilirubinate. (Book p267)

questions.q: Black pigment stones are seen in haemolytic disorders such as:
opts: G6PD, sickle cell anaemia and spherocytosis
questions.exp: Black pigment stones: seen in haemolytic disorders — G6PD, sickle cell anaemia, spherocytosis. (Book p267)

questions.q: The predominant composition of black pigment stones is:
questions.exp: Black pigment stones: composition — insoluble bilirubin pigment polymer (predominate) and calcium bicarbonate/phosphate. (Book p267)

questions.q: Which of the following is a risk factor for gallstones through lithogenic bile?
questions.exp: Risk factors — lithogenic bile: raised cholesterol, obese individuals, post ileal resection. (Book p267)

questions.q: Post ileal resection predisposes to gallstones because of:
questions.exp: Risk factors — lithogenic bile includes post ileal resection. (Book p267)

questions.q: Nucleation in gallstone formation is promoted by:
questions.exp: Risk factors — nucleation: infection, ascariasis, clonorchis, cholangitis. (Book p267)

questions.q: Which of the following causes gallstones by biliary stasis?
questions.exp: Risk factors — stasis: pregnancy, OCP. (Book p267)

questions.q: Post vagotomy predisposes to gallstones because:
opts: There is decreased vagal contraction leading to stasis
The sphincter of Oddi opens constantly
questions.exp: Risk factors — stasis: post vagotomy leads to decreased contraction of the vagus, causing stasis. (Book p267)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: On X-ray, what proportion of gallstones are radiolucent?
questions.exp: Investigation — X-ray: 90% radiolucent, 10% radiopaque. (Book p267)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: On X-ray, what proportion of gallstones are radiopaque?
questions.exp: Investigation — X-ray: 10% radiopaque. (Book p267)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: The seagull sign on X-ray is produced by:
questions.exp: Signs: seagull sign — bircusped stone. (Book p267)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: The mercedes Benz sign on X-ray is produced by:
questions.exp: Signs: mercedes Benz sign — trircusped stone. (Book p267)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: The investigation of choice for gallstones is:
questions.exp: Investigation: USG — IOC. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A gallstone on USG characteristically shows:
questions.exp: USG: post acoustic shadows. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Post acoustic shadowing on USG is ABSENT in:
questions.exp: USG: post acoustic shadow is absent in gallbladder polyp. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Asymptomatic gallstones are managed by:
questions.exp: Presentation and management: asymptomatic stones — no pain, observation. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A porcelain gallbladder is defined by:
questions.exp: Indication for surgery: a. Porcelain gallbladder — calcification of gallbladder wall. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A porcelain gallbladder raises the risk of cancer by:
questions.exp: Porcelain gallbladder: risk of cancer raised by 5-7%. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A gallbladder polyp is an indication for surgery when it is:
questions.exp: Indication for surgery: b. GB polyp — >1 cm. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Which additional feature of a gallbladder polyp strengthens the indication for surgery?
opts: Increasing size, especially with associated stones
questions.exp: GB polyp: increasing in size and associated with stones are surgical indications. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Which of the following is a listed indication for cholecystectomy in gallstone carriers?
questions.exp: Indication for surgery: c. Salmonella typhi carrier. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: In a diabetic, cholecystectomy is indicated because:
opts: The first attack of stones is severe and painful
Stones are always radiolucent in diabetics
questions.exp: Indication for surgery: d. Diabetes — first attack of stones is severe and painful. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Cholecystectomy before bariatric surgery is indicated in:
opts: The endemic zone of gallbladder cancer
questions.exp: Indication for surgery: e. Bariatric surgery — endemic zone of GB cancer. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A gallstone of what size is an indication for surgery?
questions.exp: Indication for surgery: f. >2 cm stone. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Acute cholecystitis is:
questions.exp: Acute cholecystitis: inflammation of gallbladder. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: The symptoms of acute cholecystitis include:
opts: Pain on the right side of the abdomen, nausea and vomiting, anorexia
questions.exp: Symptoms: pain in right side of abdomen, nausea and vomiting, anorexia. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Murphy's sign is:
opts: Pressing on the right hypochondrium catches the breath
questions.exp: Signs: Murphy's sign — pressing on right hypochondrium catches the breath. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: BoA's sign in acute cholecystitis is:
opts: Hyperesthesia over the region of the 10th rib
Pain in the right shoulder tip
questions.exp: Signs: BoA's sign — hyperesthesia over the region of the 10th rib. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Under the Tokyo consensus guidelines, a LOCALISED sign of inflammation in acute cholecystitis is:
opts: Murphy's sign and right upper quadrant pain
questions.exp: Tokyo consensus: A. Localised signs of inflammation — Murphy's sign, right upper quadrant pain. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A SYSTEMIC sign of inflammation in the Tokyo consensus criteria is:
opts: Fever with raised CRP and leukocytosis
questions.exp: Tokyo consensus: B. Systemic signs of inflammation — fever, raised CRP, leukocytosis. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A classical imaging feature of acute cholecystitis is:
opts: A normal wall with a small lumen
questions.exp: Tokyo consensus: C. Classical features — wall thickness >3 mm, pericholecystic fluid (due to inflammation), probe tenderness. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Pericholecystic fluid in acute cholecystitis is due to:
questions.exp: Classical features: pericholecystic fluid (d/t inflammation). (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A SUSPECTED diagnosis of acute cholecystitis (Tokyo consensus) requires:
opts: Any 1 of A plus any 1 of B
questions.exp: Dx: suspected Dx — any 1 of A + any 1 of B. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A DEFINITE diagnosis of acute cholecystitis (Tokyo consensus) requires:
opts: Any 1 of B/A plus any 1 of B plus C
questions.exp: Dx: definite Dx — any 1 of B/A + any 1 of B + C, as written in the book. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A HIDA scan is:
opts: A histamine inhibition of dilation assay
questions.exp: HIDA scan: hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scan. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: In a normal HIDA scan, the tracer:
opts: Reaches the bowel in 30 minutes in 90% of cases
Reaches the bowel in 30 minutes in 10% of cases
Reaches the bowel within 1 hour in all patients
questions.exp: HIDA scan: affinity to biliary tree — reaches bowel in 30 mins (in 90%). (Book p269)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: In acute cholecystitis, the HIDA scan shows:
opts: Only a dilated common bile duct
questions.exp: HIDA scan: acute cholecystitis — inflamed neck leads to non-visualisation of the gallbladder. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Grade III acute cholecystitis (Tokyo consensus) is defined as:
opts: Cholecystitis with a normal white cell count
questions.exp: Severity grading: Grade III — severe cholecystitis + organ dysfunction. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Which of the following places a patient in Grade II (moderate) acute cholecystitis?
opts: Duration of 24 hours with a normal mass
No local mass and no complications
questions.exp: Grade II — associated with any one of: raised WBC (>18,000/mm3), palpable tender mass in the right upper quadrant, duration >72 hrs, gangrenous cholecystitis/pericholecystic abscess/hepatic abscess/biliary peritonitis/emphysematous cholecystitis. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Grade II acute cholecystitis includes all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Mild cholecystitis with none of the listed features
A palpable tender mass in the right upper abdominal quadrant
questions.exp: Grade II: moderate cholecystitis associated with any one of the listed features — plain mild cholecystitis is Grade I. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Grade I acute cholecystitis is:
opts: Moderate cholecystitis with a tender mass
questions.exp: Severity grading: Grade I — mild cholecystitis. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: Initial management of acute cholecystitis includes:
opts: Nil per oral, IV fluids, IV antibiotics with aerobic and anaerobic cover, and analgesics
questions.exp: Management: nil per oral, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (aerobic + anaerobic cover), analgesics. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A Grade I acute cholecystitis in a patient FIT for surgery is managed definitively by:
questions.exp: Definitive management: Grade I, fit for surgery — early lap cholecystectomy. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
questions.q: A Grade I acute cholecystitis in a patient UNFIT for surgery is managed by:
opts: Antibiotics and supportive care, then observation, then lap cholecystectomy
Immediate tube cholecystostomy with no further surgery
questions.exp: Definitive management: Grade I, unfit for surgery — antibiotics and supportive care, observation, then lap cholecystectomy. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: Grade II acute cholecystitis in a centre with advanced laparoscopic technique available is managed by:
opts: Antibiotics and general supportive care with early lap cholecystectomy
questions.exp: Grade II: antibiotics and general supportive care — with advanced lap cholecystectomy technique available, early lap cholecystectomy. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: A Grade II acute cholecystitis in a patient unfit for surgery is managed by:
opts: GB drainage (tube cholecystostomy), then delayed lap cholecystectomy
questions.exp: Grade II, unfit for surgery: GB drainage — tube cholecystostomy (the tube decompresses the GB and reduces inflammation) then delayed lap cholecystectomy. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: The purpose of tube cholecystostomy in acute cholecystitis is that:
opts: The tube decompresses the gallbladder and reduces inflammation
questions.exp: Tube cholecystostomy: the tube decompresses the GB, reducing inflammation. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: Grade III acute cholecystitis with NO negative predictive factors, in an advanced centre with good performance status, is managed by:
opts: Antibiotics and supportive care with early lap cholecystectomy
questions.exp: Grade III: antibiotics and supportive care; no negative predictive factors — advanced centre with good performance status (PS) gets early lap cholecystectomy. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: Grade III acute cholecystitis WITH negative predictive factors is first managed by:
questions.exp: Grade III: with negative predictive factors — tube cholecystostomy/drainage. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: After drainage, a Grade III patient with POOR performance status is managed by:
opts: Delayed lap cholecystectomy within a week
questions.exp: Grade III with negative predictive factors: good PS — delayed lap cholecystectomy; poor PS — observation. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: Acalculous cholecystitis is defined as:
opts: Cholecystitis with a single large stone
Chronic cholecystitis with a WES sign
questions.exp: Acalculous cholecystitis: cholecystitis + no GB stone. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: Which of the following is a risk factor for acalculous cholecystitis?
opts: A patient with a Phrygian cap
questions.exp: Risk factors: ICU patient. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: Prolonged TPN predisposes to acalculous cholecystitis because:
opts: TPN causes biliary stasis leading to inflammation
questions.exp: Risk factors: prolonged TPN — TPN causes biliary stasis, leading to inflammation. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: Acalculous cholecystitis is also seen after:
questions.exp: Risk factors: post CABG. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: The clinical features of acalculous cholecystitis are:
questions.exp: Acalculous cholecystitis: C/F — same as cholecystitis. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: USG findings in acalculous cholecystitis include:
opts: Thickened GB wall and pericholecystic fluid
questions.exp: Investigation: USG (IOC) — thickened GB wall, pericholecystic fluid. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: Acalculous cholecystitis that does not improve on supportive care is managed by:
questions.exp: Management: supportive care (nil per oral, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, analgesics); no improvement — lap cholecystectomy. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
questions.q: An acalculous cholecystitis patient who is UNFIT for surgery is managed by:
questions.exp: Management: unfit — tube cholecystostomy. (Book p270)

questions.q: Chronic cholecystitis is characterised by:
questions.exp: Chronic cholecystitis: multiple episodes of cholecystitis. (Book p271)

questions.q: The clinical features of chronic cholecystitis are:
opts: Right upper quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting
questions.exp: Clinical features: right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. (Book p271)

questions.q: The WES sign on USG in chronic cholecystitis stands for:
questions.exp: Investigation: USG (IOC) — wall echo shadow (WES) sign. (Book p271)

questions.q: Histopathology of chronic cholecystitis shows all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Acute neutrophilic abscess as the defining feature
questions.exp: Histopathology: 1. Clefts (ulceration of mucosa), 2. Chronic inflammatory cells — plus Rokitansky Aschoff sinuses. (Book p271)

questions.q: Rupture of Rokitansky Aschoff sinuses leads to:
questions.exp: Rokitansky Aschoff sinuses, on rupture, cause xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis — differential diagnosis: cancer. (Book p271)

questions.q: Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis is an important differential diagnosis of:
questions.exp: Rupture of Rokitansky Aschoff sinuses — xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis; D/d: cancer. (Book p271)

questions.q: The management of chronic cholecystitis is:
questions.exp: Management: lap cholecystectomy. (Book p271)

questions.q: The causative organism of emphysematous cholecystitis is:
questions.exp: Emphysematous cholecystitis: causative organism — Clostridium. (Book p271)

questions.q: A predisposing factor for emphysematous cholecystitis is:
questions.exp: Predisposing factors: immunocompromised, diabetes. (Book p271)

questions.q: The clinical features of emphysematous cholecystitis are:
questions.exp: Clinical features: pain, fever, sepsis. (Book p271)

questions.q: On USG, emphysematous cholecystitis shows:
opts: Gas within the gallbladder and in the wall of the gallbladder
questions.exp: Investigation: USG (IOC) — gas within GB, wall of GB; also CECT. (Book p271)

questions.q: The management of emphysematous cholecystitis includes:
opts: Nil per oral, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and early lap cholecystectomy or tube cholecystostomy
questions.exp: Management: nil per oral, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (broad spectrum), early lap cholecystectomy/tube cholecystostomy. (Book p271)

questions.q: A mucocele of the gallbladder is:
opts: Aseptic dilatation of the gallbladder due to a stone impacted at the Hartmann pouch neck
A cancer of the gallbladder fundus
questions.exp: Mucocele of GB: aseptic dilatation of GB d/t stone impacted at Hartmann pouch neck. (Book p271)

questions.q: In a mucocele, the gallbladder distends because:
opts: Bile is absorbed and mucus is produced by the wall
The cystic duct is patent and fills
questions.exp: Pathophysiology: impaction of stone in the neck of GB, bile absorbed and mucus produced by the wall. (Book p272)

questions.q: On examination, a mucocele of the gallbladder shows:
opts: A fixed gallbladder mass without mobility
questions.exp: Mucocele: O/E — distended GB, pain. (Book p272)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for a mucocele of the gallbladder is:
questions.exp: Mucocele: IOC — USG. (Book p272)

questions.q: The management of a mucocele of the gallbladder is:
questions.exp: Mucocele: Mx — lap cholecystectomy. (Book p272)

questions.q: A mucocele that becomes infected turns into:
questions.exp: Mucocele, if infected, becomes empyema of GB — Mx: lap cholecystectomy. (Book p272)

questions.q: Gallstone ileus is best described as:
opts: A misnomer causing dynamic bowel obstruction
A true ileus of the colon
questions.exp: Gall stone ileus: misnomer; dynamic bowel obstruction. (Book p272)

questions.q: Gallstone ileus is secondary to:
opts: A stone in the common bile duct
questions.exp: Gall stone ileus: a° to cholecystoduodenal fistula. (Book p272)

questions.q: The clinical features of gallstone ileus are those of bowel obstruction:
questions.exp: Clinical features: bowel obstruction — obstipation, vomiting, pain. (Book p272)

questions.q: The initial investigation in gallstone ileus is:
questions.exp: Investigation: X-ray abdomen erect and supine — initial investigation. (Book p272)

questions.q: Rigler's triad in gallstone ileus consists of:
opts: Small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia and a radiopaque shadow in the right iliac fossa
Murphy's sign, BoA's sign and fever
Air under the diaphragm, free fluid and mass
questions.exp: Rigler's triad: 1. Features of small bowel obstruction, 2. Pneumobilia (air in biliary tree), 3. Radiopaque shadow in right iliac fossa. (Book p272)

questions.q: Pneumobilia in Rigler's triad means:
questions.exp: Rigler's triad: pneumobilia — air in the biliary tree. (Book p272)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for gallstone ileus is:
questions.exp: Investigation: CECT — IOC. (Book p272)

questions.q: The most common site of obstruction in gallstone ileus is:
opts: The last 2 feet (60 cm) of the ileum
questions.exp: M/c site of obstruction: last 2 feet / 60cm of ileum. (Book p272)

questions.q: Rarely, a gallstone causing gastric outlet obstruction is called:
questions.exp: Rarely, stone causing gastric outlet obstruction: Bouveret syndrome. (Book p272)

questions.q: The first step in managing gallstone ileus is:
questions.exp: Management: 1. Emergency laparotomy. (Book p273)

questions.q: At laparotomy for gallstone ileus, if there is NO peritonitis or perforation, the stone is:
opts: Milked or crushed and taken beyond the ileocaecal junction
questions.exp: Management: no peritonitis/perforation — milk the stone/crush the stone, taken beyond the ileocaecal junction. (Book p273)

questions.q: At laparotomy for gallstone ileus with peritonitis or perforation, the management is:
questions.exp: Management: peritonitis/perforation — resection and anastomosis. (Book p273)

questions.q: When the patient is stable, the second operation for gallstone ileus is:
opts: Cholecystectomy and repair of the fistula
questions.exp: Management: a. When patient is stable — 2nd surgery: cholecystectomy and repair of fistula. (Book p273)

questions.q: Mirizzi syndrome is due to:
questions.exp: Mirizzi syndrome: d/t inflammation. (Book p273)

questions.q: In Mirizzi syndrome, the inflamed gallbladder:
opts: Adheres to the common bile duct and pushes it
questions.exp: Mirizzi syndrome: GB adheres to CBD and pushes the CBD. (Book p273)

questions.q: Later, Mirizzi syndrome can progress to:
questions.exp: Mirizzi syndrome: pushes the CBD — later, fistula formation, obstructive jaundice. (Book p273)

questions.q: The clinical features of Mirizzi syndrome are:
questions.exp: Clinical features: pain, jaundice. (Book p273)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for Mirizzi syndrome is:
questions.exp: Investigation: MRCP — IOC. (Book p273)

questions.q: MRCP stands for:
opts: Magnetic resonance of the common bile duct only
questions.exp: MRCP — magnetic resonance cholangio pancreatography; a non-invasive diagnostic test. (Book p273)

questions.q: MRCP is a:
opts: Invasive test requiring a side-viewing scope
questions.exp: MRCP: non-invasive diagnostic test. (Book p273)

questions.q: The management of Mirizzi syndrome is:
questions.exp: Management: lap cholecystectomy. (Book p273)

questions.q: A partial cholecystectomy in Mirizzi syndrome is done for:
questions.exp: Management: partial cholecystectomy — densely adherent GB. (Book p273)

questions.q: Stones in the common bile duct are secondary to gallbladder stones in what proportion of cases?
questions.exp: Choledocholithiasis: stones in CBD — 90% are a° to GB stones. (Book p273)

questions.q: Primary CBD stones account for what proportion of choledocholithiasis?
questions.exp: Stones in CBD: 10% — primary CBD stones. (Book p273)

questions.q: Primary CBD stones are:
opts: Formed in the CBD and are brown pigment stones
questions.exp: Primary CBD stones: formed in CBD, brown pigment stone. (Book p273)

questions.q: Choledocholithiasis may present as:
questions.exp: Clinical features: asymptomatic. (Book p274)

questions.q: Obstructive jaundice in choledocholithiasis is due to:
opts: Obstruction of the common bile duct
questions.exp: Clinical features: obstructive jaundice (d/t obstruction of CBD). (Book p274)

questions.q: Charcot's triad is seen in:
questions.exp: Charcot's triad: seen in cholangitis (inflammation of biliary tree). (Book p274)

questions.q: Charcot's triad consists of:
opts: Intermittent pain, intermittent jaundice and intermittent fever
questions.exp: Charcot's triad: intermittent pain, intermittent jaundice, intermittent fever. (Book p274)

questions.q: Reynold's pentad is:
opts: Charcot's triad plus shock/hypotension and altered mental status
A triad of pain, fever and mass
Pentad of Rigler's triad plus two signs
questions.exp: Reynold's pentad: Charcot's triad + shock/hypotension + altered mental status. (Book p274)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for choledocholithiasis is:
questions.exp: Investigation: MRCP — IOC. (Book p274)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for CBD microliths is:
questions.exp: Investigation: IOC for CBD microliths — EUS (endoscopic ultrasound). (Book p274)

questions.q: A patient with NO history of cholangitis/pancreatitis, NORMAL LFTs and a CBD diameter of 6 mm or less on USG has:
opts: A low risk of CBD stones — proceed to lap cholecystectomy
questions.exp: Risk factors table: low risk — history (−), LFT normal, CBD diameter ≤6 mm — lap chole. (Book p274)

questions.q: A medium risk of CBD stone (history of cholangitis/pancreatitis, LFT 2x normal, CBD 8-10 mm) requires:
questions.exp: Risk factors table: medium/high risk — MRCP before Sx. (Book p274)

questions.q: A HIGH risk of CBD stone is indicated by:
opts: History of cholangitis/pancreatitis with jaundice, LFT 2x normal and CBD greater than 10 mm
A normal LFT and a 5 mm CBD
An asymptomatic patient with no history
A 7 mm CBD with no history
questions.exp: Risk factors table: high — history + jaundice (+), LFT 2x (N), CBD >10 mm — MRCP before Sx. (Book p274)

questions.q: If CBD stones are detected BEFORE lap cholecystectomy, the management is:
questions.exp: Management: 1. If CBD stones detected before lap cholecystectomy — ERCP, followed by lap cholecystectomy. (Book p274)

questions.q: ERCP stands for:
opts: Endoscopic resection of the common bile duct
questions.exp: ERCP: endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography. (Book p274)

questions.q: During ERCP, the cut (sphincterotomy) is made at the:
opts: 11 o'clock position in the Ampulla of Vater
questions.exp: ERCP: cut made at 11 o'clock position in the Ampulla of Vater. (Book p274)

questions.q: After dye is injected during ERCP, it:
questions.exp: ERCP: dye is injected and delineates the biliary tree; advantage — diagnostic + therapeutic. (Book p274)

questions.q: The advantage of ERCP is that it is:
questions.exp: ERCP: Adv — diagnostic + therapeutic. (Book p274)

questions.q: The most common complication of ERCP is:
questions.exp: ERCP complication: pancreatitis (m/c), duodenal perforation. (Book p274)

questions.q: If CBD stones are detected DURING lap cholecystectomy, the procedure continues with:
opts: Laparoscopic exploration of the CBD and stone removal
Aborting the operation and sending for ERCP later in all
questions.exp: Management: 2. CBD stones detected during lap cholecystectomy — lap exploration of CBD and stone removal. (Book p275)

questions.q: After laparoscopic CBD exploration and stone removal, the next step is:
questions.exp: Management: insert T-tube. (Book p275)

questions.q: A T-tube cholangiogram is done:
questions.exp: Management: T-tube cholangiogram at 7-10 days. (Book p275)

questions.q: If the T-tube cholangiogram shows residual stones, the T-tube is:
opts: Retained for 2-3 weeks to form a channel, then choledoscope is used to remove stones (Burhenne technique)
questions.exp: Management: residual stones present — retain T-tube for 2-3 weeks, forms a channel, choledoscope to remove stones — Burhenne technique. (Book p275)

questions.q: The Burhenne technique involves:
opts: Removing stones with a choledoscope through the matured T-tube tract
Milking stones beyond the ileocaecal junction
questions.exp: Burhenne technique: retain T-tube 2-3 weeks, channel forms, choledoscope removes the stones. (Book p275)

questions.q: If the T-tube cholangiogram shows NO residual stones, the T-tube is:
questions.exp: Management: residual stones absent — remove T-tube. (Book p275)

questions.q: CBD stones detected AFTER lap cholecystesis present with:
questions.exp: Management: 3. CBD stones detected after lap cholecystectomy — presents with pain, fever, jaundice. (Book p275)

questions.q: A CBD stone presenting within 2 years of lap cholecystectomy is classified as:
questions.exp: Within 2 yrs of lap cholecystectomy — residual/retained CBD. (Book p275)

questions.q: A CBD stone presenting MORE than 2 years after lap cholecystectomy is classified as:
questions.exp: >2 yrs of lap cholecystectomy — recurrent/primary CBD stones. (Book p275)

questions.q: The management of CBD stones after lap cholecystectomy is:
questions.exp: Management: Mx — ERCP + sphincterotomy. (Book p275)

units.title: Surgical Anatomy of the Gallbladder
units.sec: Surgical Anatomy of the Gallbladder · p265
units.guide: A distended pyriform gallbladder moves side to side and hints at periampullary cancer or mucocele, while a fixed non-pyriform mass whispers gallbladder cancer. Calot's triangle — cystic artery, cystic duct, common hepatic duct — hides the cystic lymph node of Lund, the sentinel node, and is the field dissected for the critical view of safety where the cystic artery and duct are clipped before the gallbladder comes out. Watch for Moynihan's hump: a tortuous right hepatic artery that masquerades in Calot's triangle and bleeds when mistaken.

units.title: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line
units.sec: Surface Anatomy: Cystic Plate, Rouviere's Sulcus and the R4U Line · p266
units.guide: Work above the danger line: the cystic plate, continuous with the capsule of segments 4 and 5, is exposed at the critical view of safety; Rouviere's sulcus on the undersurface marks the right posterior sectoral pedicle, and the R4U line — sulcus to segment 4 base — keeps the CBD below it out of the dissection. The gallbladder has no submucosa but rich subserosal lymphatics, which is how its cancer seeds the liver, and the Phrygian cap, a folded fundus, needs no operation.

units.title: Gallstones: Classification and Risk Factors
units.sec: Gallstones: Classification and Risk Factors · p267
units.guide: The gallbladder stores, mucins and concentrates bile — and it makes stones. Pure cholesterol stones are over 90% cholesterol and solitary, mixed stones rule overall, and pigment stones split: brown ones born of infected bile (ascariasis, clonorchiasis, cholangitis) with calcium palmitate, stearate and bilirubinate, black ones of haemolysis (G6PD, sickle cell, spherocytosis) built on an insoluble bilirubin polymer. Lithogenic bile, nucleation and stasis — obesity, ileal resection, infection, pregnancy, OCP, vagotomy — are the three engines of stone formation.

units.title: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis
units.sec: Gallstones: Diagnosis, Asymptomatic Stones and Acute Cholecystitis · p267
units.guide: Nine out of ten stones are radiolucent — the exceptions flash the seagull sign (bircusped) or the mercedes Benz sign (trircusped), and USG, the IOC, catches them by their post acoustic shadow, absent in polyps. Silent stones are observed, but the porcelain gallbladder (5-7% cancer risk), a polyp over 1 cm, the Salmonella typhi carrier, the diabetic, the bariatric candidate in an endemic zone and the stone over 2 cm all go to theatre. Acute cholecystitis — Murphy's sign, BoA's sign over the 10th rib, the Tokyo criteria A plus B suspecting and the imaging confirming — runs from mild Grade I to organ-failing Grade III, with HIDA showing the non-visualised gallbladder between.

units.title: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis
units.sec: Management by Grade and Acalculous Cholecystitis · p270
units.guide: Grade II is antibiotics and support with early lap cholecystectomy where the technique exists, otherwise tube cholecystostomy to decompress and delay; Grade III splits on negative predictive factors — early lap cholecystectomy in the fit at an advanced centre, drainage and delayed surgery for good performance status, and observation for the poor. Acalculous cholecystitis strikes the ICU patient, the prolonged-TPN patient, post CABG and septic — same signs, same USG, and when it fails to improve it needs the gallbladder out or a tube in.

units.title: Chronic and Emphysematous Cholecystitis
units.guide: Chronic cholecystitis is the story of repeated attacks — the WES sign on USG, clefts and chronic cells on the slide, and Rokitansky Aschoff sinuses that, rupturing, make xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis, a great imitator of cancer. Emphysematous cholecystitis is Clostridium in the diabetic and immunocompromised: gas in the wall on USG, sepsis in the history, and early lap cholecystectomy or drainage after broad-spectrum antibiotics.

units.title: Mucocele and Gallstone Ileus
units.guide: A stone impacted at the Hartmann pouch neck turns the gallbladder into a mucocele — aseptic, distended, mucus-filled — that becomes an empyema when infected. When the same stone grinds a cholecystoduodenal fistula, the largest one travels to the terminal ileum and causes gallstone ileus: a misnomer, really a dynamic obstruction with Rigler's triad (SBO, pneumobilia, radiopaque shadow in the right iliac fossa) on the film and CECT as the IOC. At laparotomy, milk or crush the stone unless peritonitis demands resection, and return for cholecystectomy and fistula repair when stable.

units.title: Mirizzi Syndrome
units.guide: Mirizzi syndrome is the inflamed gallbladder glued to the common bile duct, pushing it until it fistulises and obstructs — pain plus jaundice. MRCP, the non-invasive IOC, makes the diagnosis, and lap cholecystectomy (partial when the gallbladder is densely adherent) is the treatment.

units.title: Choledocholithiasis
units.guide: CBD stones are 90% secondaries from the gallbladder and 10% primary brown pigment stones. They sit silently or bring obstructive jaundice, Charcot's triad in cholangitis and Reynold's pentad when shock and confusion join. The risk table steers the low-risk straight to lap cholecystectomy and the rest to MRCP; ERCP before surgery (cut at 11 o'clock, pancreatitis its commonest complication), T-tube and the Burhenne technique when stones are found at operation, and ERCP with sphincterotomy when they appear afterwards — within 2 years a retained stone, beyond, a recurrent one.
